html:
A United States law signed by President Chester A. Arthur on 6 May 1882 that banned the immigration of Chinese labourers for ten years. It was the first US law to shut out people of a named nationality, and it lasted, renewed and tightened, until 1943.

Chinese migrants had come to California in large numbers from the Gold Rush of 1849 on. They worked in mines, farms and laundries, and built much of the western part of the first transcontinental railroad. When jobs were scarce in the 1870s, white workers and politicians in the West blamed them for low wages. Anti-Chinese riots and violence followed.

The act also barred Chinese already in the US from becoming citizens. Later laws made it permanent and forced Chinese residents to carry papers. Many came anyway as "paper sons", claiming kinship with citizens, and were questioned for weeks at the Angel Island station in San Francisco Bay. The act was repealed in 1943, when China was an ally in World War II, though only a tiny quota was allowed. It set a model for the wider immigration limits of the 1920s.
